content: Lamivudine and raltegravir are indicated for use in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 years or older who weigh at least 30 kg. The recommended dosage is one tablet (150 mg/300 mg) taken orally twice daily. The safety and efficacy of this combination have not been established in children under 6 years of age. Aluminum hydroxide decreases raltegravir levels by binding to cations in the gastrointestinal tract. This combination is contraindicated and not recommended, even with dose separation. Similarly, aluminum hydroxide/magnesium carbonate and aluminum hydroxide/magnesium trisilicate reduce raltegravir levels by enhancing gastrointestinal absorption. These combinations are also contraindicated and not recommended with or without dose separation. Magnesium-containing antacids, including magnesium hydroxide and magnesium supplements, reduce raltegravir plasma levels by forming chelates with polyvalent cations, which decreases absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. These combinations are contraindicated, and dose separation may not adequately prevent this interaction. Lamivudine should not be co-administered with emtricitabine-containing products due to the risk of therapeutic duplication and increased risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Similarly, lamivudine and emtricitabine-containing products should be avoided as they increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Raltegravir and elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir DF should not be co-administered, as elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir DF is a complete regimen for HIV and should not be combined with other antiretrovirals. Antiretroviral medications, including lamivudine and raltegravir, may interfere with the manufacturing of autologous cell-based therapies such as atidarsagene autotemcel, betibeglogene autotemcel, and lovotibeglogene autotemcel. Patients should discontinue antiretroviral therapy at least one month before cell mobilization and until all apheresis cycles are completed. Some long-acting antiretrovirals may require a longer discontinuation period for complete elimination. Co-administration of sorbitol and lamivudine should be avoided. Tafenoquine increases lamivudine levels by inhibiting organic cation transporter-2 (OCT2) and multidrug and toxin extrusion (MATE) transporters. Co-administration should be avoided, and if necessary, monitor for substrate-related toxicities and consider dosage adjustments. Lamivudine increases the levels of cabozantinib by inhibiting MRP2 transporters, which may increase cabozantinib toxicity. Close monitoring is recommended, and dosage adjustments may be necessary. Raltegravir levels are reduced by drugs such as rifampin, rifabutin, and apalutamide due to increased hepatic clearance or induction of UGT1A1 enzymes. These combinations require caution and close monitoring. Lamivudine increases the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome when combined with other antiretrovirals such as abacavir, efavirenz, atazanavir, tipranavir, and nevirapine. These combinations should be used with caution and monitored closely. Lamivudine increases the levels of erdafitinib by reducing renal clearance. Alternative therapies that are not OCT2 substrates should be considered, or the dose of OCT2 substrates should be reduced based on tolerability. Ganciclovir and valganciclovir increase the risk of hematologic toxicity when combined with lamivudine. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. Interferon alfa-2a and alfa-2b increase the risk of liver decompensation when combined with lamivudine. These combinations should be used with caution and monitored closely. Ritonavir and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir reduce raltegravir levels by inducing UGT1A1 enzymes. These combinations require caution and close monitoring. Orlistat decreases the levels of raltegravir and lamivudine by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, leading to a loss of virological control in HIV-infected patients. HIV RNA levels should be monitored frequently, and orlistat should be discontinued if an increased viral load is confirmed. Zinc and selenium reduce raltegravir levels by binding to cations in the gastrointestinal tract. Raltegravir should be administered at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after polyvalent cation-containing products. Isavuconazonium sulfate, a weak OCT2 inhibitor, may increase lamivudine levels. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown, but close monitoring is recommended. Trimethoprim increases lamivudine levels by competing for renal tubular clearance, potentially increasing toxicity. Caution and monitoring are advised. Trilaciclib, an OCT2, MATE1, and MATE-2K inhibitor, decreases lamivudine levels. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies should be considered. In summary, lamivudine and raltegravir have numerous drug interactions that may affect their efficacy and safety. These interactions require careful consideration, monitoring, and in some cases, avoidance or modification of therapy.
